utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T. The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. And so we resume. We observe and we have heard some -- we have been informally told outside the court that the accused Zupljanin is not present today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. He waived his right to be present because he is unable to be here for religious reasons. And we will soon get his written waiver from the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Morning, Your Honours, it's Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith again for the Prosecution. I thought his waiver was here. We can't start until we've got his waiver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I understand it will be filed once it's processed and registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can confirm that my client verbally and in written form sent his waiver already last Thursday, and I received information from the Detention Unit that this document had been sent to the Registry, so as far as the Defence is concerned, we can start with the proceedings while waiting for the document to be officially filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Korner, I would have thought that it would be -- having regard to what counsel has said and what the Registry has confirmed, that notionally his waiver is here. It's just that physically we don't have the document in front of us, and I think that what we presently know is sufficient. I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, it's a matter for Your Honours, obviously. I'm surprised if he knew he wasn't going to be here today that the waiver wasn't sent earlier, like on Friday. But having said that, if Your Honours are content with what Mr. Krgovic says, then certainly I'm not going to raise any problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. May we have the appearances please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've given them, but I'll say them again Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm sorry, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: For the Stanisic appearing Slobodan Zecevic and Slobodan Cvijetic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: For the Zupljanin Defence Dragan Krgovic, myself; and Eric Tully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do Your Honours want to take any note of the motion that was filed at 2.00 this morning by the Stanisic Defence before we start? I'm quite happy to carry on, but theoretically it affects what I ask this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we were notified on Saturday by the Prosecution on the number of the documents which are going to be used with the witness ST-203 which is to be established over the videolink. When we checked the list, the following -- there is seven documents which are not included on the 65 ter list, and it is our understanding that the ruling of this Trial Chamber is that the Prosecution must ask leave to amend its 65 ter list before it can be allowed to present these documents to the witnesses, and that is why we filed this motion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was Friday that we sent the list. The only extra on Saturday was -- Friday afternoon was the maps that we were going to use, and, in fact, I'm not sure we will be using. As far we're concerned, I accept Your Honours ruling, and I've been abiding by it. Any documents not on our 65 ter list are not sought to be admitted in evidence. I simply ask them to be marked for identification. And if we want them admitted properly we will file a new motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And otherwise the principle which is established in the guide-lines is that documents that have not been included in the 65 ter list can be put to the witness, but cannot be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours, but it is my understanding that what Ms. Korner is saying is that she will put the documents to the witness, have them MFI'd, and then after that, seek leave to amend the 65 ter list, which would be in fact after the fact when the witness was presented with these documents. And in case the Trial Chamber will decide to admit these documents, to give permission to the Prosecution to amend the 65 ter list, then I would assume that there might create a prejudice for the accused. That is my understanding. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, unless I'm missing something, aren't you anticipating? Shouldn't you wait to see what the specific application is when it arises?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I just wanted to act diligently in order not to -- not to leave the matter, not to address before -- at the moment when I realised what in my opinion is happening. That is why we filed this motion. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution has been alerted, and we'll see where we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think that's Colonel Basara sitting there. At least I hope its. I've never seen him, but I hope that is Colonel Basara sitting in front of Your Honours in the Belgrade office.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Via videolink] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Are you able to see and hear us here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. And thank you for making your way to the ICTY office in Belgrade as a witness. Sir, I would like you, first of all, to make the solemn declaration to the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Now, would you be so kind as to state your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am Branko Basara, father's name Petar, born on the 3rd of October, 1939.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born in the village of Otis near Sanski Most, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And you also told us that you are a colonel. Are you currently employed as a colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Colonel Basara, have you ever testified as a witness before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And have you ever testified in national proceedings relating to the armed conflict in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Colonel, what is going to happen today is that you will first be examined in chief by the Prosecution who -- but you cannot see this, but she is sitting in the -- to your right side of the courtroom. And Ms. Korner is going to examine you in chief for -- how long time, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not going to give an estimate after the last time, but I hope something in the region of two and a half hours. Two to two and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. So, Colonel, you understand that you will be examined in chief for the Prosecution for approximately two or maybe two and a half hours. Then when the Prosecutor has finished her examination-in-chief, you will then be cross-examined, first by the counsel for the accused Mico Stanisic, who is Mr. Cvijetic. And Mr. Cvijetic will use how long time, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, around three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. You have asked for three hours for cross-examination. And the next cross-examination will be by counsel for Stojan Zupljanin, Mr. Krgovic. And, Mr. Krgovic, how much time are you asking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: One hour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think we got any estimates from the Defence, and I hadn't appreciated that Mr. Cvijetic was going to take three hours. We may run into witness problems again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, am I to understand that we have this witness reserved through videolink today and tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For the moment, yes, we do, but I was clearly hoping that we would finish him, if not today then early tomorrow. As I say, I had no idea that Stanisic Defence wanted so long with him. And we've got the witness who is still to be cross-examined, plus, is it another two lined up or one? One. It's quite clear we'll never get to Ms. Hanson this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, you are aware of the fact that we, as a general rule, would expect the two Defence teams together to spend approximately as much time for cross-examination as the Prosecution has been given for examination-in-chief. Now, this is just a main rule but can I ask you if you think you can cut down your cross-examination a bit? Three hours seems to me to be quite long. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will do my very best to comply. When I said three hours, I was careful, and I have experience with videolink, I was careful to take into account that videolink examinations are a little slower. If the witness were in the courtroom, it would have been two or two half-hours, so I included a margin of 30 minutes, the net time I need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel. I trust that you will both do your best to get through your cross-examination with as little delay as possible. Well, Colonel Basara, there we go. We are ready to start. Do you have any questions that you wish to raise before the floor is given to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well then. The floor is yours, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, I want to start by just setting out the history about how you come to be testifying. Is it right that you were interviewed as a suspect by the Office of the Prosecutor, first of all on the 31st of August, 2002?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you interviewed again on the 31st of March of this year?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And yesterday at the Belgrade ICTY office, did you have a meeting with Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think you were also given by an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor a copy of the documents which you may be asked about today to look at?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Can I deal briefly, please, with your military career. Did you originally join, as it then was, the Yugoslav National People's Army, the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you -- how long -- well, in fact, perhaps I can deal with this in leading form because I don't think it will be under dispute. Did you complete the military academy in November of 1962?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then in 1973, did you also complete the command staff academy?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, retire from the army before the events of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you then hold the rank of colonel when you retired?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Were you brought back into the army in 1992 -- sorry, 1991?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I did not return. I was not brought back. I was mobilised as a reserve officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: 29th October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you were mobilised back into the JNA, where were you sent?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I was sent to Jasenovac to assume the duties of the commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And under what command did the 6th Krajina Brigade come?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: The 6th Krajina Brigade was under the command of the 10th Partisan Division and the 5th Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in October 1991, who was the head of the 5th Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: At that time it was General Uzelac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just to jump ahead for one moment, after the 12th of May when the Bosnian Serb army was established, did the 5th Krajina Corps of the JNA become the 1st Krajina Corps of the Bosnian Serb army, the VRS?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: He did stay, but I can't tell you the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. I don't think you understood the question. When the VRS was established at the 12th of May assembly, was the 5th Krajina Corps renamed the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: It did. It was renamed, but I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And by that stage had General Uzelac been replaced, and it was General Talic, General Momir Talic who was in charge of the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I know that General Talic assumed the command of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, would you please also elicit from the witness his rank when he was -- when he was called back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel, when you were mobilised in October 1991, did you still hold the same rank, that of colonel, or did you hold a higher rank?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I had the same rank of colonel, and I kept it throughout because I didn't want to become active duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you next a little bit about command issues. You say that the 6th Krajina Brigade was part of the Partisan --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just get back for a minute on the LiveNote so I get this right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The 6th Krajina Brigade was under the command of the 10th Partisan Division which came within the 5th Krajina Corps. As you were in charge of the brigade, from whom did you get your orders?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: From the establishment of the 1st Krajina Corps I received orders from the commander of the 10th Brigade, Colonel Joskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And from whom would he receive his orders?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: He received orders from the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would you ever receive orders direct from the commander of the 5th Corps, General Talic later but General Uzelac in October?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I never received orders directly from General Uzelac, nor assignments, but I did from General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why was there that change?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: The change occurred because General Talic knew me well, and he knew that he could give me short orders verbally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say he could give you short orders verbally, how would orders then normally be transmitted?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: The normal procedure would be to issue written orders and send them by mail to the commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say they were sent by mail. What methods of communication did you have with your superiors, first of all in October 1991? How would you send reports?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: In October 1991 communications were mainly by telephone and radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were your methods of communication secure ones?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: There were secure communication systems.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How often would you have to report to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: As far as reports are concerned, there was a duty officer at the brigade whose job it was to send short daily reports to the command of the division at the beginning, and later to the command of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what would have to go into those daily reports?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Important developments or incidents, if any occurred that day, and at the outset while we were in Jasenovac, they concerned mainly the materiel supplies available to the unit because there were no particular combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I should have asked you this before just for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, can you tell them where Jasenovac was -- is?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Jasenovac is across the Sava river to the north of Banja Luka right on the bank of the Sava river.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's now in what -- sorry. It's now Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: In Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Next can I turn, please, to disciplinary matters. In 1991, who was responsible for the disciplinary aspect in the brigade, the 6th Krajina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: In 1991 in Jasenovac, of course I was responsible as brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if someone was suspected of having committed a disciplinary offence, what would be the procedures?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: No, there were mostly misdemeanours, disciplinary misdemeanours of not so great importance, and I would usually be the one who pronounced disciplinary measures, because it was the state of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. What would happen -- you say it was misdemeanours. What would happen if it was more than a misdemeanour? For example, supposing an officer or a soldier refused to obey a direct order?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I never encountered such a case. Soldiers and officers alike respected me and carried out my orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you may not have in Jasenovac, but in your previous career - because we are still talking about the JNA - what were the procedures if someone refused to obey a direct order?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I never had a case in my whole military career where somebody would refuse to obey my orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any other officers who were not in the same fortunate position as you, Colonel, who did have to take such measures?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: You asked me so I replied. As for others, I can say that the procedure is such that then you would go to the superior officer, submit a report, and then go -- and then the higher command or the court under whose jurisdiction the matter was would deal with this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Was there a legal procedure involving military prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: The military prosecutor joined only in the case of serious violations or some grave crimes such as wounding or killing. In that case, this would be a matter for the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. In 1991 October the JNA was engaged in fighting in Croatia; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you take any part in any combat operations in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: My brigade was deployed in Jasenovac securing the monument marking the place where many Serbs perished in World War II. We were not in active actions in that area. We were just guarding that monument.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any situations where police and the army were engaged in combat operations in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I believe that I really am not authorised to provide any assessments of the things that I heard and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you say authorised, what do you mean; it's a military secret or that you simply don't know?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: These are matters that I am not entirely familiar with. It's just what I heard on the basis of stories, somebody telling somebody else, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Colonel, can I just ask you a question in order to be sure that we have understood fully your functions during the period. You said that the 6th Brigade had been ordered to defend the monument for fallen Serbs during the last world war. Are you saying that an entire brigade was ordered to defend a monument during a period of an armed conflict? It seems to me to be a bit excessive.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not just my brigade, but -- it was like this: It was not only my brigade that was there because we are not just talking about the monument as a building that can be defended. The area that was being defended was a broader area. There was a brigade from Dubica also deployed in that area because we had taken up the periphery of Jasenovac and an area a little bit beyond that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. Just to have an idea, how many troops, approximately, were in your brigade at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were about 1.000 men in my brigade, but the situation varied. Some would leave, then they would return, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Returning to what I was asking you about, which was combat operations involving the police, what I want to know, Colonel, is in your experience, in your very great experience as a JNA officer, under -- if there was a combat operation involving the military and elements of the police, who would be in control? Who would have the authority to issue orders?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: The authority lay with the military depending on the rank of the commander, or the rank of the person who was in command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can you explain that a bit further. What do you mean by "depending on the rank"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: It depends if it was a person of a higher rank and higher level units that were engaged, then the units were -- of the police were in a minority, so then the unit and the commander of the police would be resubordinated to the military. If the police units were more numerous and the military contingent was smaller, then the police would take charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. In time -- perhaps I should ask you this, apart from the conflicts that began in 1991 in Slovenia and then Croatia, had you ever operated before that in a time of war or imminent threat of war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. As far as you were concerned, however, in this period, staying for the moment in October to December 1991, other than combat would the military have authority over the police in the course of the police's normal civilian duties, keeping order and the like?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I was not responsible for that so I really couldn't tell you how it was regulated in the field because I was in Jasenovac constantly dealing with my own problems that I had in Jasenovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move, then, to the period of 1992. I'm going to jump ahead for a moment where there was, in the area of Sanski Most where you were based, a civilian authority made up of the Crisis Staff and the police and the military presence. Did you as the commander in that area of the brigade give orders to the police?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: No, I did not issue orders to the police because the state of war had not been declared.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Even if a state of war had been declared, would you have given orders to the police about how they should carry out non-combat duties, in other words, civilian duties?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I would not order them to carry out regular duties, but I would issue orders that had to do with combat actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. All right, Colonel, I want to move now, please, into 1992. Did you -- were you on the 1st of April, 1992, sent to the area of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we can look, please, at the order. It's 65 ter number 592, and you will find it behind divider 2 in the bundle you've got there, Colonel. Sorry, Colonel, I'm waiting just until it comes up. Is it up? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay, Colonel, is this an order signed, if we look at the third page, by Major-General Momir Talic, and dated the 1st of April?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And does that order which is sent to the command of the 10th Partisan Division -- says that the 6th Partisan Brigade is to be pulled from combat, and it gives the names of the places, and then orders you to be deployed in the Sanski Most-Kamengrad village, to mean a village area; is that right? That's on the first page.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It says you were in combat or the 6th partisan Brigade was in combat, whereabouts was that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: This was just a term. It was considered that we were in combat because we were armed, we were in Jasenovac where from time to time there were provocations from the Croatian forces so that's what this would refer to then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then it says that your tasks once you had been redeployed were to achieving full control of the territory preventing inter-ethnic conflicts, setting up roadblocks, and securing features of special importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, for some reason we were still at page 2 on the screen, so I would be grateful if we could see actually the page that you are reading from.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Colonel, did you actually -- were you sent a copy of this order, or was it simply transmitted verbally to you by the command of the 10th Partisan Division? Colonel, did you hear the question? Did you see a written copy of this order, or was it -- were you simply told verbally by the 10th Partisan Division that you should redeploy?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I received a written order from the 10th Partisan Division, and on the basis of that order, I transferred the brigade from the 3rd to the 4th April in the Sanski Most sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And were you told that you were to achieve full control of the territory?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: This is a phrase usually used in peacetime during exercises, but until the state of war is declared, the army cannot take control over the territory. Only in the places where the units are deployed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So did you query why, as there wasn't a time of war, you were meant to be achieving full control of the territory?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I didn't query it, but I just did the best that I could in the field where I was located.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever, during this period that we are now dealing -- starting to deal with, that is April through until the end of July 1992, ever query any of the orders that you received from your superiors?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I cannot remember right now if I ever did that. I probably reacted to each order that was not entirely clear, but I really couldn't tell you right now exactly which those orders were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So what, if an order wasn't completely clear, you are saying you reacted? You mean you would try and get clarification?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I understand it's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, so it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Colonel, now, when you redeployed to the Sanski Most area, did you still have, as you explained to His Honour, 1.000 men in your brigade roughly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Once we came to the Sanski Most area, there were 1.000 men. However, later people came who had not responded to the call-up when we went to Jasenovac. These people started turning up so that the strength of the brigade increased.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where were you based once you had redeployed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: There seems to be and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I think it's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My command was stationed at Lusci Palanka which is 20 kilometers from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, for interruption, but the exhibit number wasn't called. It says it was already in evidence, so we don't know which exhibit number is that. I'm sorry, it wasn't announced by the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, but -- Madam Registrar, please announce.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P60.3 was tendered on 1st October, 2009.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Just to get an idea of what the terrain looks like --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Can you go to your binder, divider number 28, and can we have up, please, 65 ter number 3110. Is it up?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Colonel, I don't think it is marked on this map, can you tell us where Luska Palanka was, is still?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Lusci Palanka in this map would be here where it says Bosanska Krupa; that's what it says here on the map. It's quite close to the boundary that has been marked. There is Skucani Vakuf, and it's that road that leads towards Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So you were based on the boundary of the municipality of Bosanska Krupa and Sanski Most; is that right? That's where your base was.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes, but it's more on the -- belonging to Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your area of responsibility there? Obviously Sanski Most. Any of the other municipalities that border Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: According to the order that was issued, none other than Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: However, did your brigade eventually, and I'm jumping ahead a little, also carry out operations in other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: My brigade, the whole brigade never carried out any combat actions anywhere. Certain battalions, however, did pursuant to orders of the corps command, and they were sent to other fronts throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. These battalions were resubordinated to the commands of tactical and operational groups in those relevant sectors of the front.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did battalions -- and just remind us how many men in a battalion.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Depending on the battalion and the part of the municipality where it was formed, depending on the density of the population, it ranged from 350 to 500 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And did battalions from your brigade in fact carry out operations, for example, in Krupa, Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: No, none of the battalions as a whole carried out actions in Bosanska Krupa except for a number of men who did participate of their own initiative in the first day of combat in Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Men who were under your command of their own initiative went off to Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you do anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I didn't because they expected, just like in World War II that Muslims from Bosanska Krupa could come to their village and kill people there again, just as they did in World War II, so they of their own initiative went to provide help to the Krupa brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but, sorry, these were -- I'm just trying to understand this. These were men who came under your command who, without any orders, you say, went off to help in Krupa. Did you take any action for this breach of discipline?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Well, you need to understand that I didn't have all of those people together under my command. They were staying at their homes. They were not mobilised. They were staying at their homes and when they heard that combat was going on, they left of their own initiative, so I couldn't establish how many people went, their names, but I did find out that a number of the men did participate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, I'm sorry, Colonel, military discipline, as you've explained to us, wouldn't that be something that was a serious breach of discipline?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: At that point, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why not? Men acting without orders?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: If you were in danger and your family was in danger, then a person has the right to try to prevent something like that from happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Maybe so, but nobody asked your permission, did they, to go and do this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: No, no, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And they should have, shouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Had they asked for permission, then probably the entire unit would have been mobilised and sent there, but nobody asked. So they just went spontaneously of their own initiative to join. I don't know to what extent they actually participated. I have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, therefore, if what you are telling us is right, Colonel, men who went off on their own initiative, you have no idea how many people you have under your command?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: At no point in time could any commander know how many men were under his command because the state of war had not been declared, so that people after executing a certain assignment would be dismissed to go home and then would be mobilised again, so that the commander often did not have one single battalion in place except at the front. Once they returned from the front, the men would be released and they would go home.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, my interest -- the interest of this case is not in Krupa, so I'm going to leave that. But one other question, then. You said they went off there in case the Muslims attacked. What proportion of the men in the battalion were non-Serb in April of 1992? Roughly. I don't expect an exact figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, while we are waiting for the connection to be re-established, I'd like to use this opportunity. I've been thinking and I would like to add to my objection of this morning. You probably did not quite understand me at first. I do not see the point of the 65 ter list if the Prosecution can at any rate show documents outside of that list to the witnesses. The Defence was informed that day or the day before that the document would be used, and the document is not on the 65 ter list. This is, of course, prejudicial to the Defence because we design our Defence based on what is on the 65 ter list. If the Prosecution now uses some documents that they did not put on the 65 ter list or will only include later, then we don't have the time, and we don't have the resources to counter with our own documents. That was the point of my objection, Your Honours, and I think this creates a really serious situation for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. May I suggest that we take this issue up for a closed discussion when we have the 65 ter meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. I agree. [In English] Your Honours, I just wanted to amend my objection in order to be clear on the record what is the essence of my objection. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, Colonel, the line has now been re-established. It was broken for a short while and the Prosecution will now resume its examination-in-chief. But, Colonel, may I remind you that given your medical condition, which is the reason why you are testifying today through videolink, the Court would like to invite you to indicate to us immediately if at any point you wish to have a short break. Normally the sessions run for 90 minutes, and so since we started at 9.00, we will have to adjourn at 10.30. And the reason for this is that the technicians need to replace the tapes for the recording of these proceedings. So every 90 minutes there needs to be a break so that the technicians can change the tapes, and the breaks are of 20 minutes length. So in 10 minutes we will have the first break which will last 20 minutes and then we will resume and go on for another 90 minutes, but if, as I said, if at any point you need to take a break irrespective of the regular breaks, you just let us know. Is that understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel, the question I asked you before we lost contact was what proportion roughly of the men under your command were non-Serb at the beginning of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Around two to three per cent of the complement of units; however, they received a directive from Sarajevo to leave the units as soon as possible so that the units remain ethnically pure, Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. What, the non-Serbs received an order from Sarajevo to leave?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Through their authorities in Sanski Most the Muslims, the SDA, they were invited to leave the units of the 6th Brigade and go home.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: These were men who had been mobilised?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: They had been mobilised earlier, but since the state of war had not been declared, they basically came and went as they pleased.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And is this right, so we understand it, no state of war was ever declared during the period that we are concerned with in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: No. It was not declared until the bombing of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, yes, considerably later. I want to look at, please, now your interaction, please, with the municipal authorities in Sanski Most. When you had been redeployed to that area, did you deal with the authorities who were in charge of Sanski Most, then the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I had contacts with the Municipal Assembly in Sanski Most as required. If I had something to settle with them, to warn them about anything or perhaps if they invited me officially to attend an assembly session or a session of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you first arrived in Sanski Most, who was president of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: There were Serbs and Muslims in the Municipal Assembly, 50 per cent of Serbs and the remaining 50 per cent were Muslims and Croats because that reflected the composition of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, you misunderstood. I asked the -- do you know the name of the person who was president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: The president of the Municipal Assembly was Nedeljko Rasula, and the president of the Executive Board was Mirza Karabeg.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to ask you to look at a record of a meeting that was apparently held on the 20th of April with yourself and General Talic and members of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, that is 65 ter -- it's already in evidence. It's P60.13.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's behind divider 3 in your binder, Colonel, and you will need to go to a page, I believe, that's 0 -- in the B/C/S, 0379441.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in the English for the purposes of coming up on the screen, it's page 15, and then on to page 16. Can we go to page 15, please, in. English. One-five.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Is that a record - I think you had a chance to read again yesterday - of a meeting that you attended, together with General Talic, Major - is that - Zekaj?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Zeljaja.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So Major Zeljaja, was he based in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it says representatives of the SDS, SDA, and HDZ. Now, was this the only meeting before the take-over that took place where General Talic attended?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I think it was the only one attended by General Talic, but I can hardly remember what was discussed and how the meeting ran.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you about two matters. But that was only one attended by General Talic. Can you remember why General Talic had come to Sanski Most that day?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Well, it was part of his work as commander to inspect units and to maintain contact with the leadership of the municipality in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There's a reference there to -- if you go a few lines down, it's the next page, page 16 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it's time for the break. Do you want to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I gather it's now being displayed apparently. I see, you want me to take a break, fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We will then take the break now and adjourn for 20 minutes and resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel, we were just waiting for the document to come up on our screen here, but I just want to ask you to look, please, at the part where somebody called, I think it's Redzo speaks, which is the top of our page 16 in English. And he says he reads the proclamation of the parties from the 15th of April, 1992, an agreement to carry out divisions in the municipality. And then there's a demand. And before we move to the next part, who was Redzo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Redzo was the president of the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that's Rasula, is it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: No, no, Rasula was the president of the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party. And this one, Redzo, was the president of the Muslim party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was his surname?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Redzo Kurbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, further down that page, on page 16, we see Mirzet speaking, where he says, "The result of the cooperation is last night's success. We received a telex from the Territorial Defence about its mobilisation, but we were in the process of reaching agreement..." "... ignore the national structure percentage..." "The SDS party is taking the SUP building, and the president says, 'You have no place here any longer.'" Now, you were aware that the previous day, Rasula had effectively, and the SDS had, taken over the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I don't know which day it was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: -- but there was an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but were you aware that there had been, in fact, a take-over that the previous day, previous evening, of the municipal building by the SDS and indeed the SUP?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Well, let me answer you briefly. I was present when they agreed to divide the MUP. There was a meeting between them, I don't know which day it was where they agreed to divide the MUP. The Serbs were supposed to stay in the MUP building, whereas the Muslim part of the MUP was to be relocated into the premises of an enterprise called Sana, and when they dispersed, nobody was arrested. The Muslims [Realtime transcript read in error "Serbs"] went to the municipal building and took it over. That's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Karabeg -- that's Mirzet, Mirzet was Mr. Karabeg, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, there was a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mirzet Karabeg was the president of the Executive Board, which means Rasula's assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you pause a moment, please, there's a matter we have to deal with internally here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 28/20, I believe the witness said different. It says here, "The Serbs went to the municipal building and took it over." I believe the witness says other thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel, so there's a query. In the end of your last answer, you explained how the Muslim part of the MUP was to be relocated into Sana. And then you said, according to our note, the Serbs went to the municipal building and took it over. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't say the Serbs went to the municipal building and took it over. I said the Muslims did that. The Muslim part of the MUP went to the municipal building and took it over.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you are saying, what, after the Muslim MUP had been dispossessed of the SUP, they took over the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: The municipal building, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Really. So what is Mr. Karabeg talking about last night's excess for? What did he mean by that? Excesses, I should think it must be.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: He meant to say that it was a success for them, taking over the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: A success, is that what the word is in -- in the original language, in the Serbian language, in that part that you are looking at? What does it say that Mr. Karabeg said? Can you read it out, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Let me just see where it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you'll find it -- all right. I tell you what, Colonel, don't worry. I can deal with this with other evidence. Leave that alone. I want you to find, however, the part where you speak which is a bit further on. Do you see your name? You will find it, I can assist on this. I think you'll find it on page 00379442. And in the English it's on page 17, sorry. Have you front the part where you've spoken, Colonel Basara?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I haven't found it. I'm just telling you what I experienced.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: The MUP of the Muslims went to the municipal building and took it over.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, so you say. All right. Can you, however, please look at the part where you spoke. It's after that part that you just looked at. It's on page -- whatever page number I gave earlier, 00379442 stamped on that page. And you are recorded as saying something, and I just want to ask you about that, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've only got part of the B/C/S on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can whoever is with you find, please, in the original B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right, you say the army did not act well in connection with the SUP. Now, what did you mean by that, please, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I don't see that, the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you read out -- do you see your name?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: What I see here -- yes, it says "Branko Basara," and then in brackets, it says "Moja Redzo" --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, further up the page from there. There's a line which says: "Colonel Basara."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's ten lines down from the top of a page of this diary which has the number 4 at the top. Which is copied on ERN number 00379442.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I don't know what he wrote down. I said that the army didn't do the best thing in relation to the SUP. We couldn't prevent them from splitting up. They split up as per agreement. I don't know what the person who wrote this was thinking.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but did you -- no, this is allegedly something you said first. Did you say something like that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: How can I remember now whether I said something then or not? So many years have passed since then. This person wrote whatever they wrote, and now I am supposed to remember whether I really said that or not. I'm just giving you my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Were you of the opinion on the 20th of April, 1992, that the army should have prevented the split of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I wasn't because we didn't have the right to that. They could split up if they decided to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can you look, please, at what General Talic said which is on the same page of the B/C/S, ERN number, but it's 5 on the diary. Fourth line from the bottom. It's page 17. On the same page as the last quote. On the bottom of page 17. General Talic said: "The JNA will guarantee the peace of the citizens, citizenry, and the security of property. We are asking for your help. Don't call anyone for help, otherwise you will have Kupres, Bosanski Brod and Vukovar." Do you see those words?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What did General --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: But I couldn't really say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Couldn't say what? Colonel, when General Talic said that, "Don't call anyone for help, otherwise you'll have Kupres, Bosanski Brod, and Vukovar," who was he saying don't call anyone for help?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one moment, I'm not receiving the interpretation anymore.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really cannot say because I don't recall him saying that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the interpreter say something, please, so that we can check if we are getting the interpretation, if they can please say anything. Can they just do a test, say 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3. They can perhaps say something so that I can see if I can hear them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The counsel is by asking the interpreters to say something so that he can confirm that he is receiving -- okay, apparently the problem is corrected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Colonel, sorry about that. Now, look, "don't call anyone for help." To whom was he speaking? The Serbs, the Muslims, the Croats, or everybody?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I think that he was addressing, but I cannot say on his behalf what he was thinking, but I assume that he was addressing everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, "you will have Kupres, Bosanski Brod, Vukovar." What had happened in those places?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: There was combat action carried out. There were conflicts between Croat and Serbs at Kupres, then at Vukovar. It's well known what happened, and there were major casualties, so he was warning the sides to try to resolve something by reaching an agreement. This is what it seemed to me to be said at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it didn't seem to you that this was a threat directed in any way at the Muslims and Croats only, is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I told you that I don't remember him saying it at all, so I really cannot now say to whom he was addressing this as a threat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. This document is already an exhibit. Can you move, now, please, to in your bundle divider number 4. It's 65 ter 605. And that's already -- sorry, it's admitted in evidence already as P60.6.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is a conclusion of the Crisis Staff of the 28th of April ordering people to hand in weapons and dealing with aircraft. In fact, ordering apparently the shooting down of aircraft. Were you ever ordered by anybody to shoot down aircraft that didn't bear a JNA symbol?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: No, I didn't receive any such orders, nor did I do anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And then item number 4: "That the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality for Sanski Most meet with the commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade, Colonel Basara, and start regulating the relationship between the armed forces of the Serbian Territorial Defence and the Yugoslav army." Now, was there such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I don't remember that it took place, so I have no idea about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What sort of regulating needed to be done between the JNA, as it still was, and the TO?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: What probably needed to be resolved was -- well, the TO staff commander was Musli Novic [phoen], he was a Muslim so they probably wanted to appoint a Serb as TO commander. So that's probably what the idea was, but I didn't take part in that, so I don't really recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, was the Muslim commander of the TO replaced by a Serb?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes. This did happen later. I just don't recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to move, then, please, because that document's already exhibited, to another meeting that took place, this time on the 14th of May. It's behind divider 6, and it's 65 ter number 796. Right. Now, you had a chance to read through this yesterday, didn't you, Colonel Basara?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I didn't look at this document yesterday. I'm seeing it now for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, didn't you go through the documents in the presence of investigator Paul Grady yesterday?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes, I did look at a lot of documents yesterday, but I don't recall seeing this one yesterday. Perhaps I flipped it over together with another document, but I don't have the impression now that I saw this document yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But you were asked about this document, weren't you, in interview way back in 2002? Anyway, don't worry. This is a meeting on the 14th of May with presidents of municipalities in the zone of responsibility of the division, that's the 30th Partisan Division. Present at the meeting Colonel Stanislav Galic. Is that the colonel who subsequently became General Galic and was involved in the siege of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then there's yourself present, the commander of the TO staff in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The president of Kljuc municipality, of Donji Vakuf, Mrkonjic Grad, Sipovo, Bugojno, and then Mr. Kalabic. As a matter of interest, why wasn't Mr. Rasula present, anybody from Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Mr. Rasula didn't attend because Sanski Most is outside of the region from where this division was formed because Rasula is in the area that was under the command of the 10th division, whereas this is the 30th division here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. So why -- why were you attending the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I don't know why I was summoned. Probably because they expected that I would be able to be of some assistance in that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, wasn't it because you were actively a battalion -- as we see under the Kljuc heading of the 6th Partisan Brigade was actually operating in Kljuc? Two battalions, in fact. If you go to the part where Kljuc is underlined, and that's on the second page of the English. And it's the second page also of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I can just explain. I can explain that I was probably called because there were about 100 men in Jasenovac from Kljuc under my command, and that's why they asked me for help when they were taking power. That's why I went there. I knew they were about to take power. I went there and provided security so that there wouldn't be a conflict or bloodshed. The whole thing happened without any bloodshed or anyone being arrested or anything like that. After that I was no longer engaged in the Kljuc area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's take that in stages, shall we. If we look at the recording of what was said about Kljuc, units from the 5th Corps, the 9th Corps, a battalion of the 6th Partisan Brigade, and a battalion of the 1st Partisan was securing Kljuc, and as you say, you went there to help, didn't you, the SDS take power?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you ordered to do that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I didn't receive an order from anyone, but in the desire to prevent inter-ethnic conflicts, I wished to contribute to a painless process because I knew they were about to take power. Had I not come, there probably would have been bloodshed. So with the help of one battalion, I managed to prevent something like that from happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So this was the Serbs illegally seizing power in Kljuc, wasn't it? The SDS, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Objection. It's a leading question. It's not cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think the Colonel has already said it. It's not cross-examination, nor is it a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that right, Colonel? Colonel, did you hear --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I really am not able to assess this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But what -- you didn't receive any orders, you say? You sent your battalion in to prevent bloodshed in Kljuc. Why would there have been bloodshed, in your view?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Most probably there would have been bloodshed because the Muslims would put up resistance or some paramilitary forces that I didn't know about, but I believed that they probably existed, could have committed some crimes. It would have led to retaliation or arrests, but nothing like that happened, so I felt that it was my humane duty, the duty as a human being to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You obviously felt that you ought to send your battalion into Kljuc to help in the taking of power. Was it your view that -- well, sorry, what was your view as to whether the SDS --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I sent a battalion not to take over power.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, to assist. I said assist. Would the SDS --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Objective was not to send a battalion to take over power, but to prevent bloodshed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Two days earlier it's right you were aware that there had been the declaration of the Army of the Serbian Republic, the VRS?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, were you aware --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- and if you don't remember the dates, that the Bosnian Serb Assembly had taken the decision to create its own army?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I found out later, but at that time I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, all right, but hang on a moment. You say that, let's go on in meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Page 3 in the English, and I think it's page 3 in the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: A paragraph that begins: "At that meeting..." "A decision was taken to name the armed forces of Krajina the Army of the Serbian Republic ..." And then further on skipping the rest of it: "The strategic goals formulated at the meeting in Banja Luka were presented." Do you remember presenting or hearing about the six strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I don't remember those goals, and I don't remember that meeting. Only on the basis of what I am reading and talking about it with you. I mean, it was a long time ago so I really couldn't say what was said, what was written down, because it just wouldn't be true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I just want to ask you one thing about that. In your view as an experienced officer in the military, was it possible to be a state separation of three national communities without bloodshed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: In the beginning, I did think that this could happen, and I tried in Sanski Most to agree, and I propose that I would secure the Podgrmec area so that people could live there just as they had lived until then. However, when what happened in Dobrovoljacka, Ulica, and Sarajevo with General Kukanjac and the rest and with those losses or casualties that occurred there, it became evident that this was something that would not really be possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And became evident, did it, fairly quickly? I mean, this is May we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I'm just saying that from that point on that's how it was. Until then, I was trying to make sure in the field that no bloodshed would occur.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's an exhibit. I don't think it is. So could that be exhibited, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P105, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, that was the 14th of May. I want you to look, please, at a document for the 21st of May, which is behind divider 5. So if you go back one, and it's 65 ter number 1597. That's a document from the 1st Krajina Corps command, dated the 21st of May, signed by the assistant commander for moral guidance, which is on the third page in English, you needn't turn it up for the moment, Colonel Vukelic. Did you know Colonel Vukelic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I knew him by sight. I'd seen him a couple of times at meetings, but I had no direct contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And he is obviously issued as apparently part of his duties, this particular document. Can you look, please, at the second page in English, and I think it's also the second page in -- no, sorry, it's the bottom of the first page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the transcript on my screen has stopped. I don't know if --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, it has, too, yes, and mine as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What is the answer to that? Do we know why it stopped? No. All right. I presume that it's still being typed up, so we will get it eventually, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it's the bottom of the first page in B/C/S, and it's the top of the second page in English. "The constituent Serbian people who live on around 65 per cent of the area and represent more than 35 per cent of the population of Bosnia must struggle for complete separation for the Muslim and Croatian peoples and form their own state. Only after that will they be able to decide with whom and how they will unite and associate. They do not want anything that is somebody else's, anything that has not been theirs for centuries, but they will not give an inch of their own territory." Now, first of all, in your position as commander, did you receive this document? Because it says --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I did not get it personally, but it's probably my assistant for political work in the brigade received it, and he must have informed me of the contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Because it pertained to my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly, it says "sent to all corps units." The commander for moral guidance, Colonel Vukelic, would he require the authority of General Talic to send out a document like this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: He needed authority from Talic, and he must have received it, and it must have been the position of the entire command. That position was advised by the superior leadership probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The view that is expressed there, "the constituent Serbian people who live on around 65 per cent of the area," et cetera, et cetera, whose view was that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: That was the view of the political leadership of the Republika Srpska that was passed on down to units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was it a view that you personally agreed with?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I did not agree with the war and all of it, but I had to accept this view because it was ordered from above.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you say this was the political -- I can't read LiveNote, can we.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, the political leadership. What was the relationship between the political leadership and the army?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I don't know that because I did not cooperate with the top layers of the leadership of Republika Srpska, so I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But was the army obliged, from your experience as a long serving army officer, to carry out the will of the political leadership?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Well, the army was duty-bound to obey because the president of the SDS, Mr. Karadzic, was at the same time president of Republika Srpska and the Supreme Commander of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then one other paragraph please, quickly. It's on page 3 in the English, and I think it's at the bottom of page 2 in the B/C/S. It's the paragraph that begins, "It will protect and defend its people..." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "... from all threats and help them in distress. It will beat the enemy in armed struggle and will conduct itself towards captured and wounded members of the enemy, as well as the civilian population, in a soldierly, civilised, and humane manner, in keeping with the norms and international laws of war." First of all, who was the enemy?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Well, who was the enemy. It was obvious who was in conflict with the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well it may be obvious -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Those were practically Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters request: Could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, it's my fault. I'm not watching when he is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "... and in conducting itself towards captured and wounded members of the enemy as well as the civilian population in a soldierly, civilised, and humane manner..." Was that actually what happened, Colonel Basara? And let's particularly deal with Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: That depended on each individual commander and certain authorities on the ground, such as authorities in municipalities. It depended on everyone's personal attitude toward the task.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm dealing with events, please, in Sanski Most directly within your area of responsibility. Did your troops conduct itself towards captured and wounded members of the enemy, as well as civilian population, in a soldierly, civilised, and humane manner?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: As far as I know. The overwhelming majority of those who were real members of the brigade conducted themselves in that way. However, there were certain exceptions that were well known, and certain steps were taken to sanction them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Will you tell us about some of these incidents that, as you say, are well known. First of all --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: For instance, there was a notorious case in the hamlet of Kenjari.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What happened there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: In that village, the battalion commander who covered that area talked to the Muslims and 17 or 18 of them accepted to come to the battalion. He had promised them uniforms and weapons. However, what happened was that the village Hrustovo was disarmed. Two soldiers were killed immediately when they approached the village, and in the meantime, those Muslims who had been waiting for him to come back were killed. One managed to escape, and he must have said to others the battalion commander knows who did this. The perpetrators were arrested, and turned over to the SUP of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Wait a minute, these people who killed the people in Hrustovo, the people killed were civilians, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: They were civilians who were waiting to be given uniforms and weapons to join the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But instead they were killed by men under your command, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Well, yes. They were killed by the men who had stayed there to guard them from that battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you say you arrested -- you had the perpetrators arrested and turned them over to the SUP?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes, they were turned over to the SUP because we didn't have a prison to hold them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what happened to them thereafter?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, did you take steps to ensure that these killers were prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I thought that once they were turned over to the professional authorities of the MUP, things would run their course. I did not intervene any longer because I was busy with other duties in the brigade, activities had intensified, and I had no time to pay attention to particular cases rather than other duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That's Hrustovo. What happened at Vrhpolje bridge?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: At Vrhpolje bridge, from what I was able to find out, when civilians were withdrawing from Hrustovo -- because that battalion commander whose two soldiers were killed said that the civilian population should withdraw to Sanski Most. One group, however, from Kljuc or wherever, happened to be there and killed a number of those civilians, but I came late to that bridge, and when I did come, I brought my police officers and they prevented further killing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
